claims.text: A conventionally tempered martensitic steel can be engineered to exhibit a reproducible ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed transition can be produced by exploiting intrinsic temper-embrittlement behavior within a narrow temperature window.
Baseline impurities in the proposed martensitic steel naturally promote grain-boundary segregation during tempering.
Adjusting tempering temperature controls the degree of grain-boundary segregation.
Deliberately adjusting phosphorus or tin content controls the degree of grain-boundary segregation.
Impurity segregation changes grain-boundary chemistry and cohesion.
Within a specific tempering-temperature range, impurity segregation at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes a sudden drop in ductility.
Below the embrittlement window, segregation is insufficient and the alloy is ductile.
Above the embrittlement window, segregation is reversed and the alloy regains ductility.
Mechanical testing will show high ductility at low temperatures, brittle behavior within a narrow intermediate temperature range, and recovered ductility at higher temperatures.
Tempered martensitic steel typically has high ductility outside the embrittlement range.
The proposed behavior is restricted to conventional impurity-susceptible martensitic steels.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys may not exhibit the transition because they lack pronounced impurity-segregation effects.
The optimum impurity concentration, embrittlement-temperature range, and transition rate vary with alloy composition and processing history.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies a marked ductile–brittle–ductile transition, whereas the baseline says the same general material has no significant ductile–brittle transition. The intended distinction between untreated baseline material and the impurity/thermal-treatment intervention is not made fully explicit.
